Let $Q$ be the amount of reactant in the reactor at time $t.$ Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in seconds. This is equal to the rate at which reactant enters the reactor minus the rate at which reactant leaves the reactor.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{g}/\text{s}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which reactant enters the reactor.

First, note that pure solvent (i.e., a solution containing $0\,\text{g/mL}$ of reactant) enters the reactor at a rate of $90\,\text{mL/s}.$ So, the rate at which the *reactant* enters the reactor is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}})\cdot (90\,\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mL}}})\cdot (90\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mL}}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which reactant exits the reactor.

To find the rate at which reactant leaves the reactor, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reactor at time $t.$

The reactor initially contains $7\,500\,\text{mL}$ of solution; pure solvent enters at $90\,\text{mL/s},$ and mixed solution leaves at $60\,\text{mL/s}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reactor after $t$ seconds is 

$$
V(t)=7\,500+90t-60t=30(250+t)\,\text{mL}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reactor is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of reactant in the reactor, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{30(250+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $60\,\text{mL/s},$ *reactant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(60\,\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{s}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{30(250+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}}) \\  & =(60\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mL}}}{\text{s}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{30(250+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mL}}}) \\  & =\frac{2Q}{250+t}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{2Q}{250+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{2}{250+t}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{250+t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{2}{250+t})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-2\int \frac{1}{250+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-2(\operatorname{ln}⁡|250+t|)+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(250+t)^{-2}|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|(250+t)^{-2}|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(250+t)^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the reactor initially contains $98\,\text{g}$ of reactant. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=98,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =98 \\ \frac{A}{(250+0)^{2}} & =98 \\ A & =98(250)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =\frac{98(250)^{2}}{(250+t)^{2}} \\  & =98{(\frac{250}{250+t})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reactor begins to overflow. The reactor has a capacity of $10\,500\,\text{mL},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=10\,500$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =10\,500 \\ 30(250+{t}_{o}) & =10\,500 \\ 250+{t}_{o} & =350 \\ {t}_{o} & =100\,\text{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the amount of reactant in the reactor at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(100) & =98{(\frac{250}{250+100})}^{2} \\  & =98{(\frac{250}{350})}^{2} \\  & =98{(\frac{5}{7})}^{2} \\  & =50\,\text{g}.\end{aligned}
$$
